title: Item Embedding
summary:
An item embedding **encodes each item (document, product, image, user) as a vector** so that a computer can compare items by geometry.

Two families:
- **Dense** vectors (typically 64-1,536 floats, every dimension non-zero) come from a trained model. Dimensions have no individual meaning, but items with similar meaning end up close together, so "cheap car" lands near "affordable automobile".
- **Sparse** vectors (one-hot, bag-of-words, TF-IDF, BM25 weights) have one dimension per vocabulary term and are mostly zeros. They are exact, interpretable and great for rare tokens such as SKUs and error codes, but blind to synonyms.

Production rules:
- **One space.** Items and queries must be embedded by the *same model and version*. Mixing v1 and v2 vectors is meaningless; a model upgrade means re-embedding the whole corpus (dual-write the new index, then switch).
- **Memory** is `items x dims x bytes`: 10M x 768 x 4 B (float32) is about 30.7 GB. Quantizing to int8 or product quantization cuts it 4x to 30x+ at some recall cost.
- **Embed offline** for items, online only for the query.
- **Hybrid** retrieval (dense + sparse) often beats either alone.

Once you have vectors you need a [similarity](#/sd/f/similarity) measure and a [similarity search](#/sd/f/similarity-search) index; user attributes used for exact rules belong in [user context](#/sd/f/user-context) instead.

drills.q: A catalogue has 10,000,000 items with 768-dimensional float32 embeddings (4 bytes per number). Ignoring index overhead, how many gigabytes (1 GB = 1e9 bytes) do the raw vectors take?
drills.explain: 10,000,000 x 768 x 4 B = 30.72e9 B = 30.72 GB. Storing them as int8 would be one quarter of that, 7.68 GB, before recall effects.

drills.q: Your search team releases embedding model v2. To save time, new documents are embedded with v2 while old documents keep their v1 vectors, and the query is embedded with v2. What do you expect?
options: Good results, because both models are trained on similar data
Query-to-old-document scores are meaningless, because the two models define unrelated vector spaces; re-embed the corpus or keep two indexes
Results only slightly worse because cosine similarity normalizes the difference
A runtime error because the dimensions differ
drills.explain: Each model learns its own coordinate system. Even with the same dimensionality, numbers from v1 and v2 are not comparable, and nothing errors, so quality silently drops. Migrate with a parallel index and a cut-over.

drills.q: Users search a help centre. Which queries favour a dense embedding retriever over a sparse (BM25) one? Select all that apply.
options: "how do I get my money back" against an article titled "Refund policy"
"ERR_CONN_4412" against an article mentioning exactly that error code
"cancel plan" against an article that says "terminate your subscription"
A query in German against English articles, using a multilingual model
drills.explain: Dense vectors capture meaning, paraphrase and cross-language similarity. An exact rare token like an error code is where sparse term matching wins, which is why hybrid search is common.

drills.q: Put the stages of an embedding-based retrieval system in order.
items: Choose an embedding model and fix its version
Embed every item offline and store the vectors in an index
Embed the user's query with the same model at request time
Search the index for the nearest vectors
Return (and optionally re-rank) the matching items
drills.explain: The index is only valid for the model that built it. Query-time work is one embedding call plus one search.

drills.q: Compare a dense and a sparse item representation, and say one operational risk of dense embeddings.
drills.answer: Dense: short learned vector, all dimensions non-zero, captures meaning (synonyms, languages), not interpretable. Sparse: one dimension per term, mostly zeros, interpretable and exact for rare tokens, no synonym handling. Operational risk: vectors from different model versions are incompatible, so a model upgrade needs a full re-embed and a parallel index; memory also scales as items x dims x bytes.
